name: Ephedrine/caffeine (ECA stack)
lead: The ECA stack is a combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin that bodybuilders and physique-focused dieters have used as a fat-loss and energy aid. People take it while cutting to get leaner: lower body fat makes muscle definition, the jawline and facial contours more visible, and the appetite suppression and extra energy are meant to make a calorie deficit easier to sustain.[1][2] Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant that works mainly by prompting the release of norepinephrine, and caffeine has been described as acting synergistically with it, which is why combination products appeared.[1]

The stack grew out of the long history of ephedra (ma huang), a plant used in Chinese medicine for roughly two thousand years, and of ephedrine, first synthesized in 1885. In the 1990s ephedra-and-caffeine supplements became some of the best-selling weight-loss products in the United States, until a run of deaths and adverse-event reports led the FDA to ban ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements on April 12, 2004.[1][3] A federal appeals court upheld the rule in 2006, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 2007.[3] The stack is therefore discussed today mostly as a historical bodybuilding staple and in regions where ephedrine remains available by other routes.

A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported that ephedrine, with or without caffeine, taken for roughly 4 to 24 weeks was associated with about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo, with a higher heart rate in users.[1] A government-commissioned meta-analysis (RAND, 2003) described modest short-term weight loss and too little data on long-term loss or on athletic performance.[3] Reported adverse effects include insomnia, anxiety, raised blood pressure and fast heart rate, and in serious cases stroke and heart attack.[1][3] Users on looksmax.org have written ECA guides framing it as a cutting aid to be paired with exercise, and caution against it for people with heart problems.[4] Forum members on T Nation recall ephedrine-based cutting supplements as the products they rated most highly before the ban.[5]

paras: ECA stands for ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. Community guides describe it as a stack for raising metabolism, suppressing appetite and boosting energy during dieting.[4] Wikipedia describes it as popular among bodybuilders who aim to reduce body fat before competitions.[1] On T Nation, members have also mentioned adding ephedrine and aspirin to a caffeine-containing routine for leaning out.[6]

In looksmaxxing terms the stack belongs to the leanness toolkit. Proponents say body-fat reduction is among the quickest ways to sharpen the face, and a stimulant-assisted cut is one route people have used alongside diet and training. The stack changes no bone or soft-tissue structure; its role is to support the fat-loss process described in the angle above.[2][4]

Wikipedia's ephedra article notes that ephedra was sold for weight loss sometimes combined with aspirin and caffeine, while the original product formulations varied widely.[3] U.S. supplements lacked standardization requirements, and the ephedrine-alkaloid content of the same brand varied by as much as ten-fold between lots.[3]

Ephedrine induces release of norepinephrine, which indirectly activates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors. It also slows gastric emptying, and thermogenesis is thought to occur mainly in skeletal muscle in adults, since adults have little brown fat.[1] Oral bioavailability is about 88 percent, onset after an oral dose is 15 to 60 minutes, and the elimination half-life is about 6 hours, with roughly 60 percent excreted unchanged in urine.[1] In monoamine-release data it is far more potent at releasing norepinephrine than dopamine and has negligible serotonin activity.[1]

Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and is widely used as an ergogenic aid; meta-analyses report improved endurance performance, and randomized trials report improved muscular endurance, strength and power with caffeine.[7][8][9] Wikipedia states that caffeine and theophylline act synergistically with ephedrine, which is the stated rationale for the combination.[1]

Ephedra (ma huang) is documented in Chinese medicine from the Han dynasty, used for asthma and bronchitis, and the article on ephedra describes use for more than 2,000 years.[1][3] Japanese chemist Nagai Nagayoshi first synthesized ephedrine in 1885. Merck began marketing it in China in the 1920s, and Chinese exports to the West rose from 4 to 216 tonnes between 1926 and 1928.[1] It entered US medical use in 1926.[1]

In the 1990s ephedra products were sold without standardization; the FDA proposed limiting products to under 8 mg of ephedrine alkaloids per serving and requiring stronger warnings in 1997.[3] The industry-formed Ephedra Education Council opposed the changes, and Metabolife, the top-selling brand, had received more than 14,000 adverse-event complaints that were not initially given to the FDA.[3] The FDA withdrew parts of the proposal in 2000, the year a New England Journal of Medicine review documented sudden cardiac deaths and disabilities, many in young adults taking labeled amounts.[3] Metabolife co-founder Michael Ellis was later sentenced to six months in federal prison for failing to report adverse events.[3]

On February 17, 2003, Baltimore Orioles pitcher Steve Bechler, 23, died after collapsing during spring training the previous day with a body temperature reported at 108 F.[13] The Broward County medical examiner attributed the death to several factors, including a liver condition, mild hypertension, his weight, heat and humidity, low food intake and ephedra toxicity.[13] The case drew congressional attention; the FDA urged consumers to stop using ephedrine-alkaloid products on December 30, 2003 and issued a final rule banning ephedrine-alkaloid supplements on April 12, 2004.[3][13]

In April 2005 a Utah federal judge (Tena Campbell), ruling for Nutraceutical Corporation, found the FDA had not shown low doses to be unsafe, which lifted the ban in Utah. The Tenth Circuit reinstated it nationwide on August 17, 2006, citing an administrative record of 133,000 pages, and the Supreme Court declined review on May 14, 2007.[3]

Ephedrine alone is described as producing modest short-term weight loss, mainly fat, with unknown long-term effects. Caffeine and other methylxanthines have been reported to act synergistically with it.[1] A 2021 systematic review reported around 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks, with heart rate rising, LDL cholesterol falling, HDL rising and no statistically significant blood pressure difference.[1] Wikipedia's article on ephedra cites a 6-month randomized trial of herbal ephedra and caffeine and describes the extra loss as roughly 0.9 kg per month versus placebo; whether the loss was maintained was not tested.[3]

A review commissioned by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services found modest short-term weight loss and insufficient data on performance enhancement, even though athletes widely use ephedrine.[3] A 2006 survey cited on Wikipedia found nearly half of collegiate hockey players had used ephedra, believing it improved performance.[3]

Reported effects of ephedrine include insomnia, anxiety, headache, hallucinations, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, reduced appetite and urinary retention. Stroke and heart attack have been reported as serious events, and combining it with MAO inhibitors can cause hypertensive crisis.[1] By 2004 the FDA had received more than 18,000 adverse-event reports linked to ephedrine products.[1] A 2000 New England Journal of Medicine review described sudden cardiac deaths and severe disability, many in young adults using labeled doses, and a 2003 Annals of Internal Medicine study reported ephedrine alkaloids were far more likely than kava or ginkgo to cause a significant adverse reaction.[3]

Caffeine has its own documented effects on sleep. A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 studies found caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and a 2017 review reported reduced slow-wave sleep.[10][11] A T Nation member recalled being unable to sleep until about 2 a.m. after taking ephedrine in the evening.[12] The looksmax.org guide states that the stack should not be used by people with heart problems.[4]

United States: ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements are banned (2004). Herbal ma huang as a pure herb or tea and ephedra extract without ephedrine alkaloids remain legally sold, and pseudoephedrine is sold under purchase limits set by the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act signed March 6, 2006.[1][3] Canada: Health Canada issued a voluntary recall in January 2002 of products above 8 mg per dose, those combined with other stimulants such as caffeine, and those marketed for weight loss or bodybuilding; 8 mg tablets remain available as natural health products.[1] Australia: ephedrine is Schedule 4 (prescription-only). Germany: sold freely until 2001, with all ephedrine-containing products prescription-only since April 2006.[1] South Africa moved ephedrine to Schedule 6 in May 2008.[1] Availability varies by country.[4]

Ephedrine is banned by the IOC and WADA (urine threshold 10 micrograms per mL), the NCAA, NFL, MLB and the PGA.[1][3] Notable sport cases cited on Wikipedia include Diego Maradona at the 1994 World Cup, motorcycle racer Noriyuki Haga in 2000 and NFL player Todd Sauerbrun in 2006.[3]

The Wikipedia summary cites a 2021 systematic review of ephedrine, with or without caffeine, reporting about 2 kg additional weight loss versus placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.[1] A 6-month randomized trial of herbal ephedra with caffeine (Boozer et al., 2002) is cited for modest weight loss versus placebo, and a RAND meta-analysis commissioned by the U.S. government reached similar conclusions on short-term loss.[3] No studies specific to appearance outcomes in lean, physique-focused users were found. Studies of caffeine alone cover endurance performance, strength and sleep.[7][8][9][10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the stack is discussed in a how-to guide aimed at fat loss while cutting, and on T Nation ephedrine comes up in recollections of pre-ban cutting supplements and in physique logs.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: ECA raises metabolism and suppresses appetite for fat loss
claims.believers: The guide author describes it as a stack for metabolism, appetite suppression and energy that assists weight-loss efforts.[4] A T Nation member says the ephedrine-based cutting supplements were the ones that really worked before the US ban.[5]
claims.experts: A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia found about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.[1] A government-commissioned meta-analysis found modest short-term loss and insufficient long-term data.[3]

claims.claim: Leaner means a sharper face and more visible muscle
claims.believers: Cutting-focused users describe the stack as a cutting aid, and body-fat loss is widely discussed in these communities as the route to visible definition.[2][4]
claims.experts: No published study has measured facial or physique appearance outcomes from ephedrine and caffeine; trials report weight loss in kilograms.[1][3]

claims.claim: It is only worthwhile alongside exercise
claims.believers: The guide says using it without exercising is pointless and compares it to taking a painkiller without pain.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies were found that test this specific claim.

claims.claim: It is safe if you have no heart problems
claims.believers: The guide warns against use with heart conditions and implies healthy users are acceptable.[4]
claims.experts: Reported effects include raised blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack, and sudden cardiac deaths have been described in young adults using labeled amounts; the FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid supplements in 2004.[1][3]

claims.claim: Caffeine plus ephedrine is more effective than either alone
claims.believers: The guide presents the three ingredients together as one stack rather than as separate products.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that caffeine and theophylline act synergistically with ephedrine; the 2021 review pooled trials of ephedrine with or without caffeine rather than comparing them directly.[1]

claims.claim: The 2004 ban removed the best cutting supplements
claims.believers: T Nation members recall pre-ban ephedrine products fondly and say nothing sold since has matched them.[5]
claims.experts: The FDA and courts cited adverse-event reports, deaths and lot-to-lot variation in alkaloid content; the Tenth Circuit upheld the rule in 2006.[3]

card.summary: A classic ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin cutting stack with modest reported fat-loss effects and a long regulatory history.
card.note: Ephedrine-alkaloid supplements are banned in the US; cardiovascular events have been reported.

quick.overview:
ECA combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is used in bodybuilding and physique communities as a cutting aid for appetite suppression and energy.

A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks.
quick.mechanism: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant; caffeine has been reported to act synergistically with it.
quick.risks: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack. The FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid supplements in 2004; legal status varies elsewhere.
